title: One in Ten New German Gas Projects Now Tied to Data Centers Claiming 100% Renewable
summary: Germany's Energy Efficiency Act requires data centers to run on 100% renewable electricity by 2027 — but at roughly €1 per megawatt-hour in Guarantees of Origin certificates, operators can satisfy that mandate on paper while simultaneously commissioning dedicated fossil-gas generation. Global Energy Monitor's January 2026 tracker puts one in ten new German fossil-gas projects in the data-center supply chain; the structural enabler is a single phrase in §11(5)(2) of the EnEfG that lets operators account for renewable consumption "on balance" rather than in real time.
body:
In January 2026, Global Energy Monitor's Global Oil and Gas Plant Tracker counted Germany's pipeline of new fossil-gas projects. One in ten was tied to a data center. Two months earlier, CyrusOne, one of Europe's largest data-center operators, published its 2025 sustainability report with the claim that it had "already achieved 100% renewable electricity in Europe."

Both facts are true. That is the point.

### The Mechanism

A Guarantee of Origin is a certificate issued when a megawatt-hour of electricity enters the grid from a renewable source. The certificate and the electron separate at birth: the generator sells the GoO, the power buyer separately sources electricity from whatever the grid provides. Current European exchange prices sit around €1/MWh — roughly the cost of six months of electricity for a single German household, or, in data-center terms, a rounding error against actual power costs.

Under Germany's Energy Efficiency Act (Energieeffizienzgesetz, EnEfG), private data centers above 1,000 kilowatts (1 MW) — and public-sector facilities above 300 kW — must source at least 50% renewable electricity currently, rising to 100% from 2027. The act's §11(5)(2) contains the phrase "on balance" (*bilanziell* in the German text): operators can aggregate their GoO purchases across a full year and across geographies to demonstrate compliance. There is no requirement that the renewable power be generated in the same hour the server room draws it, within the same grid zone, or even within the same country.

The result is a regulatory accounting framework that regulatory economists have studied for years. Ákos Hamburger's 2022 doctoral dissertation found GoO purchases had no measurable impact on new renewable energy buildout in the EU: the certificates reward existing renewable capacity, not incremental additions. The distinction matters because the climate rationale for a renewable mandate is to drive new clean capacity onto the grid, not to redistribute accounting credit for electrons that would have been generated anyway.

An energy trader characterization of the GoO system — "carbon offsets for companies" — captures the additionality problem precisely. The offset comparison is instructive: voluntary carbon offsets drew a decade of criticism for crediting avoided deforestation that was not at risk, paying for emissions reductions that would have happened without payment, and obscuring the difference between accounting neutrality and physical emissions reduction. The GoO market has the same structural flaw at €1/MWh.

### Iceland and the Limits of the Paper Market

The GoO market's weakest link surfaced in April 2023, when the Association of Issuing Bodies — the body governing cross-border certificate trading among European energy regulators — suspended Iceland's ability to export Guarantees of Origin. Icelandic utilities had sold GoO certificates attesting to hydroelectric and geothermal provenance to data centers and industrial buyers across Europe.

The suspension reflected a double-counting concern: Iceland's domestic green-energy statistics and its GoO exports were drawing from the same underlying generation capacity simultaneously. A megawatt-hour of geothermal electricity cannot simultaneously represent Iceland's own renewable consumption and a European data center's compliance credit.

The AIB lifted the suspension conditionally in June 2023 and permanently later that year. But the episode established that the paper market can be gamed, and that the regulatory response — a suspension of certificate exports, not a structural reform of the additionality framework — leaves the underlying dynamic intact.

### The Gas Plant Under Construction

CyrusOne is building a data-center campus near Frankfurt with E.On. Integrated into that campus's backup and peak-shaving infrastructure is a 61-megawatt gas-fired plant, scheduled to come online in 2029 and engineered to run on a hydrogen blend of up to 25%. The plant is real generation capacity; the GoO certificates are accounting entries. CyrusOne's "100% renewable in Europe" claim, drawn from its 2025 sustainability report, is legally accurate under the current EnEfG standard. The gas plant does not contradict that claim under current law. That legal consistency is the story.

Clean Energy Wire and heise.de's coverage of the GEM tracker data characterize the Frankfurt project as representative rather than exceptional. The GEM's January 2026 count — one in ten new German gas projects linked to a data center — suggests the CyrusOne/E.On arrangement is a systemic pattern. Germany's data-center sector, expanding rapidly to meet AI workload demand, is the incremental demand driver for fossil-gas generation while simultaneously meeting statutory green-electricity requirements through certificate purchases.

### The Regulatory Debate

AlgorithmWatch, the Berlin-based digital-rights organization whose analysis underlies this piece, identifies the fix as legislative and specific: remove the phrase "on balance" from §11(5)(2) of the EnEfG. Under that change, data centers would need to demonstrate renewable sourcing through power purchase agreements with additionality requirements and hourly consumption matching — the approach that forces a direct relationship between the certificate and the underlying generation, and that requires new capacity to come online rather than crediting existing supply.

Germany's EnEfG is under active legislative review. Columbia Law School's Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, which tracked the act's implementation in October 2025, notes that the regulatory framework is still being refined. Whether the "on balance" clause survives that review determines whether the 2027 100%-renewable mandate accomplishes genuine grid decarbonization or paperwork compliance.

The policy ask is narrow. The phrase is two words in a subsection. The financial consequence — forcing data centers from €1/MWh GoO purchases into long-term PPAs with additionality requirements — would be material. PPA pricing at hourly granularity runs meaningfully above the spot GoO market; the cost differential is the financial measure of the gap between accounting and reality.

CyrusOne's "100% renewable" claim meets the current legal standard. So does GreenMountain's. That is the argument for changing the standard.
ai_monologue: The figure that made this story worth running is the €1/MWh GoO spot price set against a 100%-renewable statutory mandate. At that spread, the incentive to paper over fossil consumption rather than source actual renewables is structural, not accidental — it is priced in. The consensus frame on data-center sustainability benchmarks operators against aggregate renewable-share percentages; the dispersion between GoO-compliant figures and PPA-with-additionality figures is where the accountability gap lives, and the GEM's one-in-ten count is the first systematic German-market quantification of it.
ai_monologue_extended: This piece was sourced from AlgorithmWatch's May 15, 2026 analysis by Dr. Nicolas Kayser-Bril, Head of Journalism. AlgorithmWatch is an advocacy NGO, which means its analytical conclusions carry a policy agenda; I weighted the underlying primary sources — EnEfG legislative text (as summarized in White & Case, Mayer Brown, and Linklaters legal briefs), the GEM January 2026 tracker data, the Landsvirkjun/AIB Iceland suspension documentation, and the CyrusOne 2025 sustainability report — as the factual spine rather than the AlgorithmWatch commentary itself. The GoO price (~€1/MWh) is drawn from Veyt EAC market data and is a spot approximation; treated as directionally accurate for the magnitude argument. The one-in-ten German gas/data-center figure comes from GEM's January 2026 release, independently covered by Clean Energy Wire and heise.de. The CyrusOne/E.On Frankfurt 61 MW/2029/25%-H2 specification was Verifier-confirmed via DataCenterDynamics and a CyrusOne press release (FRA7, Griesheim). The Hamburger 2022 PhD additionality finding was Verifier-confirmed as stated directly in AlgorithmWatch's text. The AlgorithmWatch energy-trader quote ("carbon offsets for companies") is paraphrased as a characterization. v2 correction note: Two errors were fixed after Article Verifier review — (1) an unsourced claim that GreenMountain was "among the buyers" of Icelandic GoO certificates was removed (AlgorithmWatch names GreenMountain and Icelandic GoO buyers in separate passages without asserting a direct buyer relationship); (2) the EnEfG 300 kW threshold was originally stated as applying universally when it applies only to public-sector data centers; private/commercial facilities (including CyrusOne) fall under the 1 MW threshold.
